title: Bilinear Forms and Inner Products

:::lede
So far we have studied vector spaces equipped only with their linear structure. Adding geometric notions—length, angle, orthogonality—requires additional data: an *inner product*. This structure brings abstract linear algebra closer to Euclidean geometry, while revealing that many geometric intuitions extend far beyond $\RR^n$.

We begin with the general notion of a bilinear form, then specialize to the symmetric positive-definite case (inner products over $\RR$) and its complex analogue (Hermitian inner products over $\CC$). We then study the operators adapted to an inner product—adjoints and self-adjoint, normal, orthogonal, and unitary operators—and prove the spectral theorems. Next we return to bilinear forms without any positivity: symmetric forms, which we classify over $\CC$ and $\RR$, and skew-symmetric (symplectic) forms. The chapter ends with tensor products and multilinear algebra, which turn bilinear and multilinear maps into linear ones.
:::

## <span class="num">9.1.1</span> Bilinear Forms

Before defining inner products, we study the broader class of bilinear forms. This generality clarifies which properties of inner products come from bilinearity alone and which require symmetry or positivity.

:::definition{9.1.1} Bilinear form
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $k$. A ***bilinear form*** on $V$ is a map $b : V \times V \to k$ that is linear in each variable:

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $b(\lambda v, w) = \lambda b(v, w) = b(v, \lambda w)$ for all $\lambda \in k$, $v, w \in V$.
2. $b(u + v, w) = b(u, w) + b(v, w)$ for all $u, v, w \in V$.
3. $b(u, v + w) = b(u, v) + b(u, w)$ for all $u, v, w \in V$.
:::

:::note
A bilinear form is *not* a linear map $V \times V \to k$. If we view $V \times V$ as a vector space (the external direct sum $V \oplus V$), a linear map would satisfy $b(\lambda(v, w)) = \lambda b(v, w)$, i.e., $b(\lambda v, \lambda w) = \lambda b(v, w)$. But bilinearity gives $b(\lambda v, \lambda w) = \lambda^2 b(v, w)$. The correct domain for linearizing bilinear maps is the tensor product $V \otimes V$, constructed in Section [9.8](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products).
:::

:::definition{9.1.2} Symmetric, skew-symmetric, and alternating forms
A bilinear form $b$ on $V$ is:

- ***Symmetric*** if $b(v, w) = b(w, v)$ for all $v, w \in V$.
- ***Skew-symmetric*** if $b(v, w) = -b(w, v)$ for all $v, w \in V$.
- ***Alternating*** if $b(v, v) = 0$ for all $v \in V$.
:::

:::note
Every alternating form is skew-symmetric: expanding $0 = b(v + w, v + w) = b(v, v) + b(v, w) + b(w, v) + b(w, w)$ gives $b(v, w) = -b(w, v)$. Conversely, if $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$, a skew-symmetric form is alternating, since $b(v, v) = -b(v, v)$ gives $2b(v, v) = 0$. In characteristic $2$ the two notions differ: there $-1 = 1$, so skew-symmetric means symmetric, and the dot product on $k^2$ is skew-symmetric but not alternating ($b(e_1, e_1) = 1$).
:::

:::example{9.1.3} The standard dot product
On $k^n$, the map $b(v, w) = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i w_i$ is a symmetric bilinear form. This is the “dot product” familiar from calculus.
:::

:::example{9.1.4} A skew-symmetric form
On $k^2$, define $b((x_1, x_2), (y_1, y_2)) = x_1 y_2 - x_2 y_1$. This equals $\det \begin{pmatrix} x_1 & y_1 \\ x_2 & y_2 \end{pmatrix}$ and is alternating, hence skew-symmetric. Over $\RR$, it computes the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors.
:::

### Matrix Representation

Let $V$ be finite-dimensional with a basis $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$. A bilinear form $b$ is determined by the values $a_{ij} = b(e_i, e_j)$: by bilinearity, $$b\left(\sum_i x_i e_i, \sum_j y_j e_j\right) = \sum_{i,j} x_i y_j \, b(e_i, e_j) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij} x_i y_j.$$ Writing $x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)^t$ and $y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)^t$ as column vectors, this is $$b(x, y) = x^t A y,$$ where $A = (a_{ij})$ is the ***matrix of $b$*** with respect to the chosen basis. Conversely, every $n \times n$ matrix $A$ defines a bilinear form by this formula, so the values $a_{ij}$ can be chosen freely.

:::proposition{9.1.5} Symmetry and the matrix
<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $b$ is symmetric if and only if $A = A^t$.
2. $b$ is skew-symmetric if and only if $A = -A^t$.
:::

:::proof
We have $b(v, w) = v^t A w$ and $b(w, v) = w^t A v = (w^t A v)^t = v^t A^t w$, since a $1 \times 1$ matrix equals its transpose. So $b(v, w) = b(w, v)$ for all $v, w$ iff $v^t A w = v^t A^t w$ for all $v, w$, iff $A = A^t$ (take $v = e_i$, $w = e_j$). The skew-symmetric case is the same with a sign.
:::

The matrix of a bilinear form depends on the basis, and it changes differently from the matrix of an operator.

:::proposition{9.1.6} Change of basis for bilinear forms
Let $\mcB = (e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ and $\mcB' = (e_1', \ldots, e_n')$ be bases of $V$, and let $P = (p_{ij})$ be the change-of-basis matrix, so that $e_j' = \sum_i p_{ij} e_i$. If $A$ and $A'$ are the matrices of a bilinear form $b$ in the bases $\mcB$ and $\mcB'$, then $$A' = P^t A P.$$
:::

:::proof
$a'_{kl} = b(e_k', e_l') = b\left(\sum_i p_{ik} e_i, \sum_j p_{jl} e_j\right) = \sum_{i,j} p_{ik}\, a_{ij}\, p_{jl} = (P^t A P)_{kl}$.
:::

:::note
Matrices related by $A' = P^t A P$ with $P$ invertible are called ***congruent***. Compare with $A' = P^{-1} A P$ for operators (Corollary [5.3.4](/notes/math-55a/5-3-change-of-basis#corollary-5-3-4)): the two notions agree when $P^t = P^{-1}$, which will be the case for change of basis between orthonormal bases (Section [9.5](/notes/math-55a/9-5-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators)). Since $P$ is invertible, congruent matrices have the same rank, and $\det A' = \det(P)^2 \det A$.
:::

### Bilinear Forms and the Dual Space

There is a natural connection between bilinear forms and linear maps to the dual space.

:::proposition{9.1.7} The map $\varphi_b : V \to V^*$
Given a bilinear form $b : V \times V \to k$, define $\varphi_b : V \to V^*$ by $$\varphi_b(v) = b(v, \cdot) \in V^*,$$ i.e., $\varphi_b(v)$ is the linear functional $w \mapsto b(v, w)$. Then $\varphi_b$ is a linear map.
:::

:::proof
For $v_1, v_2 \in V$ and $\lambda \in k$, and every $w \in V$: $$\varphi_b(v_1 + \lambda v_2)(w) = b(v_1 + \lambda v_2, w) = b(v_1, w) + \lambda b(v_2, w) = (\varphi_b(v_1) + \lambda \varphi_b(v_2))(w).$$ So $\varphi_b(v_1 + \lambda v_2) = \varphi_b(v_1) + \lambda \varphi_b(v_2)$.
:::

:::theorem{9.1.8} Bilinear forms and $\Hom(V, V^*)$
Let $B(V)$ denote the vector space of bilinear forms on $V$. The map $b \mapsto \varphi_b$ is an isomorphism of vector spaces $$B(V) \xrightarrow{\sim} \Hom(V, V^*).$$ Its inverse sends $\varphi \in \Hom(V, V^*)$ to the bilinear form $b(v, w) = \varphi(v)(w)$.
:::

:::proof
The map is linear: $$\varphi_{b + \lambda b'}(v)(w) = b(v, w) + \lambda b'(v, w) = (\varphi_b + \lambda \varphi_{b'})(v)(w).$$ Given $\varphi \in \Hom(V, V^*)$, the map $b_\varphi(v, w) = \varphi(v)(w)$ is linear in $v$ because $\varphi$ is linear, and linear in $w$ because $\varphi(v) \in V^*$; so $b_\varphi \in B(V)$. By construction $\varphi_{b_\varphi} = \varphi$ and $b_{\varphi_b} = b$, so the two maps are inverse to each other.
:::

:::note
In the language of Chapter 8, this isomorphism is natural. A linear map $f : V \to W$ induces maps in the opposite direction, $$\begin{aligned}
B(W) &\to B(V), & b &\mapsto b(f(\cdot), f(\cdot)), \\
\Hom(W, W^*) &\to \Hom(V, V^*), & \varphi &\mapsto f^t \circ \varphi \circ f,
\end{aligned}$$ which make $V \mapsto B(V)$ and $V \mapsto \Hom(V, V^*)$ contravariant functors on $\mathbf{Vect}_k$ (Definition [8.2.5](/notes/math-55a/8-2-functors-and-natural-transformations#definition-8-2-5)). The isomorphisms $b \mapsto \varphi_b$ form a natural transformation between them (Definition [8.2.9](/notes/math-55a/8-2-functors-and-natural-transformations#definition-8-2-9)): for $b \in B(W)$ and $v, v' \in V$, $$\varphi_{b(f(\cdot), f(\cdot))}(v)(v') = b(f(v), f(v')) = \varphi_b(f(v))(f(v')) = \big(f^t \circ \varphi_b \circ f\big)(v)(v').$$
:::

:::definition{9.1.9} Rank and nondegeneracy
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional. The ***rank*** of a bilinear form $b$ is $\rank(\varphi_b) = \dim(\Img(\varphi_b))$. The form $b$ is ***nondegenerate*** if $\varphi_b$ is an isomorphism.
:::

:::note
Let $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$ be a basis of $V$ with dual basis $\{e_1^*, \ldots, e_n^*\}$, and let $A$ be the matrix of $b$. Then $\varphi_b(e_j) = b(e_j, \cdot) = \sum_i b(e_j, e_i)\, e_i^*$, so the matrix of $\varphi_b$ in these bases is $A^t$. Hence $\rank b = \rank A^t = \rank A$, and $b$ is nondegenerate iff $A$ is invertible. Since $\dim V = \dim V^*$, $\varphi_b$ is an isomorphism iff it is injective, so nondegeneracy means: if $b(v, w) = 0$ for all $w \in V$, then $v = 0$. As $A$ is invertible iff $A^t$ is, this is equivalent to the same condition with the roles of the two variables exchanged.
:::

:::proposition{9.1.10} Dimension of the space of bilinear forms
If $\dim V = n$, then $\dim B(V) = n^2$.
:::

:::proof
We have $B(V) \cong \Hom(V, V^*)$ by Theorem [9.1.8](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#theorem-9-1-8), and $\dim \Hom(V, V^*) = n \cdot n = n^2$ since $\dim V^* = n$. Alternatively, $b \mapsto A$ is an isomorphism from $B(V)$ to the space of $n \times n$ matrices, since the entries of $A$ can be chosen freely.
:::

## <span class="num">9.1.2</span> Inner Products over the Reals

To do geometry, we need more than bilinearity. The key additional properties are symmetry (so that $b(v, w) = b(w, v)$) and positive-definiteness (so that “length” is always nonnegative).

:::definition{9.1.11} Inner product (real case)
Let $V$ be a vector space over $\RR$. An ***inner product*** on $V$ is a bilinear form $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle : V \times V \to \RR$ satisfying:

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. **Symmetry:** $\langle v, w \rangle = \langle w, v \rangle$ for all $v, w \in V$.
2. **Positive-definiteness:** $\langle v, v \rangle \geq 0$ for all $v \in V$, with equality iff $v = 0$.

A real vector space equipped with an inner product is called a (real) ***inner product space***.
:::

:::note
Positive-definiteness only makes sense over an *ordered* field, where “$\geq 0$” is meaningful. In practice, this means $\RR$. We cannot directly define inner products over $\CC$ or finite fields using this definition; we will see the complex workaround shortly.
:::

:::example{9.1.12} The standard inner product on $\RR^n$
The dot product $$\langle v, w \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i w_i = v^t w$$ is an inner product. Symmetry is clear, and $\langle v, v \rangle = \sum v_i^2 \geq 0$ with equality iff all $v_i = 0$.
:::

:::example{9.1.13} A weighted inner product
On $\RR^n$, for constants $c_1, \ldots, c_n > 0$, define $$\langle v, w \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i v_i w_i.$$ This is an inner product: it is clearly bilinear and symmetric, and $\langle v, v \rangle = \sum c_i v_i^2 \geq 0$, with equality iff all $v_i = 0$ because every $c_i > 0$. Different weights emphasize different coordinates.
:::

:::proposition{9.1.14} Inner products are nondegenerate
If $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is an inner product on $V$, the map $V \to V^*$, $v \mapsto \langle v, \cdot \rangle$, is injective. In particular, if $V$ is finite-dimensional, every inner product on $V$ is nondegenerate.
:::

:::proof
Suppose $\langle v, w \rangle = 0$ for all $w \in V$. Taking $w = v$, we get $\langle v, v \rangle = 0$. By positive-definiteness, $v = 0$.
:::

:::note
The converse is false: a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form need not be positive-definite. For example, the Minkowski form $b(v, w) = v_1 w_1 - v_2 w_2 - v_3 w_3 - v_4 w_4$ on $\RR^4$ is nondegenerate and symmetric, but $b(v, v)$ can be negative. Such forms are classified in Section [9.6](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms).
:::

## <span class="num">9.1.3</span> Hermitian Inner Products over the Complex Numbers

Why can’t we directly use the same definition over $\CC$? If $b$ is a bilinear form on a complex vector space, then $b(iv, iv) = i^2 b(v, v) = -b(v, v)$. So if $b(v, v) > 0$, then $b(iv, iv) < 0$: bilinearity and positive-definiteness are incompatible over $\CC$.

The solution is to weaken bilinearity: we require linearity in one variable and only *conjugate*-linearity in the other.

:::definition{9.1.15} Sesquilinear form
A map $H : V \times V \to \CC$ on a complex vector space $V$ is ***sesquilinear*** if, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \CC$:

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $H(u + v, w) = H(u, w) + H(v, w)$ and $H(u, v + w) = H(u, v) + H(u, w)$.
2. $H(\lambda u, v) = \ol{\lambda} H(u, v)$.
3. $H(u, \lambda v) = \lambda H(u, v)$.

That is, $H$ is conjugate-linear in the first argument and linear in the second.
:::

:::note
This is the convention of Artin (and of most physics texts). Some authors, including Axler, use the opposite convention: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The two conventions are exchanged by swapping the arguments, $H(u, v) \leftrightarrow H(v, u)$, so every formula in one convention has a counterpart in the other; but formulas from the two conventions must not be mixed.
:::

:::definition{9.1.16} Hermitian form
A sesquilinear form $H$ on a complex vector space $V$ is ***Hermitian*** (or ***conjugate-symmetric***) if $$H(u, v) = \ol{H(v, u)}$$ for all $u, v \in V$.
:::

:::note
Conjugate-symmetry implies $H(v, v) = \ol{H(v, v)}$, so $H(v, v) \in \RR$ for all $v$. This makes positive-definiteness meaningful.
:::

:::definition{9.1.17} Hermitian inner product
A ***Hermitian inner product*** on a complex vector space $V$ is a Hermitian form $H : V \times V \to \CC$ that is **positive-definite**: $H(v, v) \geq 0$ for all $v$, with equality iff $v = 0$. A complex vector space with a Hermitian inner product is a (complex) ***inner product space***.
:::

:::example{9.1.18} The standard Hermitian inner product on $\CC^n$
Define $$H(z, w) = \sum_{i=1}^n \ol{z_i}\, w_i = z^* w,$$ where $z^* = \ol{z}^t$ is the conjugate transpose (a row vector). Then $H$ is sesquilinear, and:

- $H(w, z) = \sum \ol{w_i}\, z_i = \ol{\sum \ol{z_i}\, w_i} = \ol{H(z, w)}$.
- $H(z, z) = \sum |z_i|^2 \geq 0$, with equality iff $z = 0$.
:::

:::note
If $H$ is a Hermitian form on a finite-dimensional space with basis $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$, let $h_{ij} = H(e_i, e_j)$ and $A = (h_{ij})$. Then $$H\left(\sum_i x_i e_i, \sum_j y_j e_j\right) = \sum_{i,j} \ol{x_i}\, y_j\, h_{ij} = x^* A y,$$ and conjugate-symmetry says $h_{ji} = \ol{h_{ij}}$, i.e., $A^* = A$. A matrix with $A^* = A$ is called ***Hermitian***; conversely, every Hermitian matrix $A$ defines a Hermitian form $x^* A y$ on $\CC^n$.
:::

**Convention.** From now on, an ***inner product space*** is either a real vector space with an inner product or a complex vector space with a Hermitian inner product. We write $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ in both cases and let $k \in \{\RR, \CC\}$ be the scalar field. Over $\RR$, complex conjugation is the identity, so every statement below specializes to the real case by ignoring the bars. In both cases, $$\langle \lambda u, v \rangle = \ol{\lambda} \langle u, v \rangle, \qquad \langle u, \lambda v \rangle = \lambda \langle u, v \rangle, \qquad \langle u, v \rangle = \ol{\langle v, u \rangle}.$$

The map $v \mapsto H(v, \cdot)$ is no longer linear, and we need a version of rank–nullity for such maps.

:::lemma{9.1.19} Conjugate-linear maps
Let $V$ and $U$ be complex vector spaces. A map $f : V \to U$ is ***conjugate-linear*** if $f(u + v) = f(u) + f(v)$ and $f(\lambda v) = \ol{\lambda} f(v)$ for all $u, v \in V$, $\lambda \in \CC$. If $f$ is conjugate-linear, then $\ker f$ and $\Img f$ are subspaces, and if $V$ is finite-dimensional, $$\dim V = \dim \ker f + \dim \Img f.$$ A composite of two conjugate-linear maps is linear, and a composite of a linear map and a conjugate-linear map (in either order) is conjugate-linear.
:::

:::proof
Let $\ol{U}$ be the set $U$ with the same addition and with the new scalar multiplication $\lambda \star u = \ol{\lambda} u$. Since complex conjugation is a field automorphism of $\CC$ ($\ol{\lambda + \mu} = \ol\lambda + \ol\mu$, $\ol{\lambda\mu} = \ol\lambda\,\ol\mu$, $\ol 1 = 1$), the vector space axioms for $\ol U$ follow from those of $U$. A subset of $U$ is closed under all operations $u \mapsto \lambda \star u$ iff it is closed under all $u \mapsto \ol\lambda u$, i.e., under all scalar multiplications; so $U$ and $\ol U$ have the same subspaces. A list $(u_i)$ is a basis of a subspace in $U$ iff it is one in $\ol U$, because $\sum \lambda_i \star u_i = \sum \ol{\lambda_i} u_i$ and $\lambda \mapsto \ol\lambda$ is a bijection; so dimensions agree. Finally, $f(\lambda v) = \ol\lambda f(v) = \lambda \star f(v)$, so $f : V \to \ol U$ is linear, and the claims about $\ker f$ and $\Img f$ follow from rank–nullity (Theorem [6.1.12](/notes/math-55a/6-1-kernel-and-image#theorem-6-1-12)). The statements about composites are immediate: two conjugations cancel, $\ol{\ol\lambda} = \lambda$.
:::

:::proposition{9.1.20} The map $\varphi_H : V \to V^*$
Let $H$ be a Hermitian form on a complex vector space $V$. For $v \in V$, the map $H(v, \cdot) : w \mapsto H(v, w)$ is linear, so $\varphi_H(v) = H(v, \cdot)$ lies in $V^*$. The map $\varphi_H : V \to V^*$ is **conjugate-linear**: $$\varphi_H(\lambda v) = \ol{\lambda}\, \varphi_H(v).$$ We call $H$ ***nondegenerate*** if $\varphi_H$ is injective, i.e., if $H(v, w) = 0$ for all $w$ implies $v = 0$. A Hermitian inner product is nondegenerate, and if $V$ is finite-dimensional and $H$ is nondegenerate, then $\varphi_H$ is bijective.
:::

:::proof
The functional $H(v, \cdot)$ is linear because $H$ is linear in its second argument, and for all $w$, $\varphi_H(\lambda v)(w) = H(\lambda v, w) = \ol\lambda H(v, w)$. If $H$ is positive-definite and $H(v, w) = 0$ for all $w$, then $H(v, v) = 0$, so $v = 0$. If $V$ is finite-dimensional and $\varphi_H$ is injective, Lemma [9.1.19](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#lemma-9-1-19) gives $\dim \Img \varphi_H = \dim V = \dim V^*$, so $\varphi_H$ is also surjective.
:::

Combining the real and complex cases, we obtain the fundamental fact that every linear functional on a finite-dimensional inner product space is “inner product with a vector.”

:::theorem{9.1.21} Riesz representation
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional inner product space. For every $\ell \in V^*$ there is a unique $u \in V$ such that $$\ell(w) = \langle u, w \rangle \quad \text{for all } w \in V.$$ Equivalently, the map $\Phi : V \to V^*$, $\Phi(u) = \langle u, \cdot \rangle$, is a bijection. It is linear if $k = \RR$ and conjugate-linear if $k = \CC$.
:::

:::proof
Over $\RR$, $\Phi = \varphi_b$ for the bilinear form $b = \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$, which is nondegenerate by Proposition [9.1.14](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#proposition-9-1-14), so $\Phi$ is an isomorphism. Over $\CC$, $\Phi = \varphi_H$ is a conjugate-linear bijection by Proposition [9.1.20](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#proposition-9-1-20).
:::

## <span class="num">9.1.4</span> Norms and the Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality

An inner product induces a notion of length via the norm.

:::definition{9.1.22} Norm
Let $V$ be an inner product space. The ***norm*** of a vector $v \in V$ is $$\|v\| = \sqrt{\langle v, v \rangle}.$$ This is well-defined since $\langle v, v \rangle$ is a nonnegative real number.
:::

:::definition{9.1.23} Orthogonality
Vectors $v, w \in V$ are ***orthogonal***, written $v \perp w$, if $\langle v, w \rangle = 0$ (equivalently, $\langle w, v \rangle = \ol{\langle v, w \rangle} = 0$).
:::

:::proposition{9.1.24} Basic properties of the norm
<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $\|v\| \geq 0$, with equality iff $v = 0$.
2. $\|\lambda v\| = |\lambda| \|v\|$ for $\lambda \in k$.
3. (Pythagorean theorem) If $v \perp w$, then $\|v + w\|^2 = \|v\|^2 + \|w\|^2$.
:::

:::proof
(i) is positive-definiteness. (ii) $\langle \lambda v, \lambda v \rangle = \ol\lambda \lambda \langle v, v \rangle = |\lambda|^2 \|v\|^2$. For (iii): $$\|v + w\|^2 = \langle v + w, v + w \rangle = \|v\|^2 + \langle v, w \rangle + \langle w, v \rangle + \|w\|^2 = \|v\|^2 + \|w\|^2,$$ since $\langle v, w \rangle = 0 = \langle w, v \rangle$.
:::

The Pythagorean theorem suggests that orthogonal vectors behave like the legs of a right triangle. More generally, since $\langle v, w \rangle + \langle w, v \rangle = 2\operatorname{Re}\langle v, w \rangle$, $$\|v - w\|^2 = \|v\|^2 + \|w\|^2 - 2\operatorname{Re}\langle v, w \rangle.$$ In a real inner product space, comparing with the law of cosines suggests defining the angle $\theta$ between nonzero vectors by $\cos \theta = \langle v, w \rangle / (\|v\| \|w\|)$. For this we first need to know that $|\langle v, w \rangle| \leq \|v\| \|w\|$, so that the ratio lies in $[-1, 1]$.

:::theorem{9.1.25} Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
For all $u, v$ in an inner product space, $$|\langle u, v \rangle| \leq \|u\| \|v\|,$$ with equality iff $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent.
:::

:::proof
If $u = 0$, both sides are $0$ and $u, v$ are dependent. Assume $u \neq 0$. Replacing $u$ by $u / \|u\|$ multiplies both sides by $1/\|u\|$ and does not change linear dependence, so we may assume $\|u\| = 1$.

Decompose $v$ along $u$: $$v = v_1 + v_2, \qquad v_1 = \langle u, v \rangle u, \qquad v_2 = v - \langle u, v \rangle u.$$ Then $\langle u, v_2 \rangle = \langle u, v \rangle - \langle u, v \rangle \langle u, u \rangle = 0$, so $v_2 \perp u$ and hence $v_2 \perp v_1$. By the Pythagorean theorem, $$\|v\|^2 = \|v_1\|^2 + \|v_2\|^2 \geq \|v_1\|^2 = |\langle u, v \rangle|^2 \|u\|^2 = |\langle u, v \rangle|^2.$$ Taking square roots gives $|\langle u, v \rangle| \leq \|v\| = \|u\| \|v\|$.

Equality holds iff $v_2 = 0$, i.e., iff $v \in \operatorname{span}(u)$, i.e. (as $u \neq 0$) iff $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent.
:::

:::definition{9.1.26} Angle between vectors
For nonzero vectors $v, w$ in a real inner product space, the ***angle*** $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ between them is defined by $$\cos \theta = \frac{\langle v, w \rangle}{\|v\| \|w\|}.$$ The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality ensures this ratio lies in $[-1, 1]$.
:::

:::corollary{9.1.27} Triangle inequality
For all $u, v$ in an inner product space, $$\|u + v\| \leq \|u\| + \|v\|.$$
:::

:::proof
$$\begin{aligned}
\|u + v\|^2 &= \|u\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}\langle u, v \rangle + \|v\|^2 \\
&\leq \|u\|^2 + 2|\langle u, v \rangle| + \|v\|^2 \\
&\leq \|u\|^2 + 2\|u\|\|v\| + \|v\|^2 = (\|u\| + \|v\|)^2. 
\end{aligned}$$
:::

## <span class="num">9.1.5</span> Orthogonal Complements

Orthogonality makes sense for any bilinear or Hermitian form, not only for inner products.

:::definition{9.1.28} Orthogonal complement
Let $b$ be a bilinear form on a vector space $V$, or a Hermitian form on a complex vector space $V$, and let $S \subseteq V$ be a subset. The ***orthogonal complement*** of $S$ is $$S^\perp = \{v \in V : b(v, w) = 0 \text{ for all } w \in S\}.$$ For an inner product, $S^\perp = \{v \in V : \langle v, w \rangle = 0 \text{ for all } w \in S\}$.
:::

:::proposition{9.1.29} Basic properties of orthogonal complements
<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $S^\perp$ is a subspace of $V$ (even if $S$ is not).
2. $S \subseteq T \implies T^\perp \subseteq S^\perp$.
3. If $b$ is symmetric, skew-symmetric, or Hermitian, then $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
4. $\{0\}^\perp = V$, and $V^\perp = \ker \varphi_b$. For an inner product, $V^\perp = \{0\}$.
:::

:::proof
(i) If $v_1, v_2 \in S^\perp$ and $\lambda$ is a scalar, then for any $w \in S$, $$b(v_1 + \lambda v_2, w) = b(v_1, w) + \lambda' b(v_2, w) = 0,$$ where $\lambda' = \lambda$ for a bilinear form and $\lambda' = \ol\lambda$ for a Hermitian form.

(ii) is immediate. (iii) If $w \in S$ and $v \in S^\perp$, then $b(w, v)$ equals $b(v, w)$, $-b(v, w)$, or $\ol{b(v, w)}$, which is $0$ in each case; so $w \in (S^\perp)^\perp$. (iv) The first two statements are the definitions, and the last is Proposition [9.1.14](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#proposition-9-1-14) (or Proposition [9.1.20](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#proposition-9-1-20)).
:::

:::note
For a general bilinear form (neither symmetric nor skew-symmetric), we must distinguish “left-orthogonal” ($b(v, w) = 0$ for all $w \in S$) from “right-orthogonal” ($b(w, v) = 0$ for all $w \in S$). For symmetric, skew-symmetric, and Hermitian forms these coincide.
:::

The key result is that an inner product space decomposes as $V = S \oplus S^\perp$ for any subspace $S$. We first count dimensions.

:::lemma{9.1.30} Dimension of the orthogonal complement
Let $b$ be a nondegenerate bilinear form, or a nondegenerate Hermitian form, on a finite-dimensional space $V$, and let $S \subseteq V$ be a subspace. Then $$\dim S^\perp = \dim V - \dim S.$$ If $b$ is an inner product, then moreover $S \cap S^\perp = \{0\}$.
:::

:::proof
Consider the composition $$V \xrightarrow{\varphi_b} V^* \xrightarrow{r} S^*,$$ where $\varphi_b(v) = b(v, \cdot)$ and $r : V^* \to S^*$ is restriction, $r(\ell) = \ell|_S$. The restriction $r$ is the dual map of the inclusion $S \hookrightarrow V$, which is injective, so $r$ is surjective (Corollary [6.2.16](/notes/math-55a/6-2-duality#corollary-6-2-16)). The kernel of $r \circ \varphi_b$ is exactly $S^\perp$.

Since $\varphi_b$ is bijective (by nondegeneracy) and $r$ is surjective, $r \circ \varphi_b$ is surjective. It is linear for a bilinear form and conjugate-linear for a Hermitian form, so in either case rank–nullity (Theorem [6.1.12](/notes/math-55a/6-1-kernel-and-image#theorem-6-1-12), or Lemma [9.1.19](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#lemma-9-1-19)) gives $$\dim S^\perp = \dim V - \dim S^* = \dim V - \dim S.$$

For the second claim: if $v \in S \cap S^\perp$, then $\langle v, v \rangle = 0$, so $v = 0$ by positive-definiteness.
:::

:::theorem{9.1.31} Orthogonal decomposition
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional inner product space and $S \subseteq V$ a subspace. Then $$V = S \oplus S^\perp.$$
:::

:::proof
An inner product is nondegenerate (Proposition [9.1.14](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#proposition-9-1-14) or Proposition [9.1.20](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#proposition-9-1-20)), so by the lemma, $\dim S + \dim S^\perp = \dim V$ and $S \cap S^\perp = \{0\}$. Hence $$\dim(S + S^\perp) = \dim S + \dim S^\perp - \dim(S \cap S^\perp) = \dim V.$$ So $S + S^\perp = V$, and the sum is direct since $S \cap S^\perp = \{0\}$.
:::

:::corollary{9.1.32} Double orthogonal complement
Let $b$ be a nondegenerate symmetric, skew-symmetric, or Hermitian form on a finite-dimensional space $V$ (for instance an inner product). Then $(S^\perp)^\perp = S$ for every subspace $S \subseteq V$.
:::

:::proof
By Proposition [9.1.29](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#proposition-9-1-29)(iii), $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$, and by Lemma [9.1.30](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#lemma-9-1-30) applied twice, $\dim (S^\perp)^\perp = \dim V - (\dim V - \dim S) = \dim S$.
:::

:::example{9.1.33} Standard orthogonal complement in $\RR^n$
Let $V = \RR^n$ with the standard inner product. If $S$ is a subspace, then $S^\perp$ is the “usual” orthogonal complement: the vectors perpendicular to every vector in $S$.

For instance, if $S = \operatorname{span}((1, 0, 0))$ in $\RR^3$, then $S^\perp = \{(0, y, z) : y, z \in \RR\}$.
:::

:::example{9.1.34} Skew-symmetric forms can have $S^\perp = S$
Let $V = k^2$ with the skew-symmetric form $b((x_1, x_2), (y_1, y_2)) = x_1 y_2 - x_2 y_1$ of Example [9.1.4](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#example-9-1-4), which is nondegenerate (its matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$ is invertible). Let $S$ be the line spanned by a nonzero vector $v$.

For any $w \in k^2$, we have $b(v, w) = 0 \iff \det(v \mid w) = 0 \iff w \in \operatorname{span}(v) = S$.

So $S^\perp = S$. In particular, $S \cap S^\perp = S \neq \{0\}$, and $V \neq S \oplus S^\perp$. This cannot happen for inner products.
:::
